study_identification_part.si4_title: Nomograms of human hippocampal volume shifted by polygenic scores

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To examine the impact of genetic adjustment using hippocampal volume polygenic scores (HV-PGS) on hippocampal volume nomograms and investigate the translational ability to detect dementia patients, demonstrating how accounting for polygenic effects in normative modeling can help untangle phenotypic heterogeneity.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: ANOVA tests comparing HV percentiles produced with genetically adjusted vs. unadjusted nomograms to assess whether genetic adjustment significantly differentiates groups (F>19; p<8.04E-6). Analysis of median percentile differences between high and low PGS subgroups within each diagnostic category to quantify variance reduction (e.g., 90% relative reduction in CN group percentile gap). Cox proportional hazards models for longitudinal MCI-to-AD conversion, accounting for sex and age, using percentiles from both adjusted and unadjusted nomograms as predictors (hazard ratio 0.97; beta -0.03; p<4.87E-08). Comparison of percentile distributions across diagnostic groups (CN, MCI, AD) using median and SD. Visual inspection of subject positions relative to nomogram quantiles (e.g., 2.5%, 50% quantiles).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Genetic adjustment using HV-PGS shifted nomograms by ~100 mm³ (equivalent to ~3 years of normal aging at age 65), significantly reducing intra-diagnostic-group variance by an average of 68% relative decrease in ADNI cohort, though it did not improve MCI-to-AD conversion prediction.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using 35,686 UK Biobank subjects, GPR nomograms extended the applicable age range by 20 years (45-82 years) compared to the sliding window approach (52-72 years), enabling evaluation of 86% vs. 56% of ADNI subjects. Polygenic scores for HV explained up to 28% of variance (R²=0.28 at p-value threshold 0.75 for bilateral HV in combined sexes). Stratifying by top and bottom 30% of HV-PGS shifted nomograms upward and downward respectively by ~50 mm³ each (total difference ~100 mm³, or 2.3% of mean HV), which corresponds to approximately 3 years of normal aging for a 65-year-old. ANOVA tests confirmed significant differences between adjusted and unadjusted percentiles (F>19; p<8.04E-6). In the ADNI validation cohort, genetic adjustment reduced the percentile gap between high and low PGS subjects: CN group showed 90% relative reduction (from 10% gap to 1% gap), MCI showed 60% relative reduction, and AD showed 56% relative reduction, with an average of 68% relative decrease in intra-diagnostic-group variance. However, Cox proportional hazards models found no significant difference in MCI-to-AD conversion prediction between genetically adjusted and non-adjusted nomograms (both hazard ratio 0.97; p<4.87E-08). The GPR approach proved data-efficient, achieving similar accuracy with only 5% (900 samples) of the dataset as with the full training set. Male HV declined faster (-20.3 mm³/year) than female HV (-14.6 mm³/year), with peaks observed at 50 years (males) and 53.5 years (females).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: The study identified several limitations: (1) Stratification-based approach for PGS adjustment rather than direct integration into GP models; (2) PGS susceptibility to site effects from genotyping and imputation quality; (3) Use of a single GWAS for bilateral HV in both sexes, whereas sex-specific GWASs might improve accuracy; (4) Reliability concerns with FreeSurfer HV estimates (known to overestimate HV, significant differences from manual segmentation); (5) Potential for improved results with other brain regions having higher SNP heritability (e.g., cerebellum, whole brain); (6) Large variance in PGS estimates may undermine stratification effectiveness; (7) Possible remaining site effects despite NeuroCombat harmonization; (8) Suspected edge effects in younger age ranges (e.g., peak in male nomogram likely due to under-sampling in younger participants).
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: While this study has shown the significant impact of PGSs on HV nomograms, we have identified areas for improvement. Integrating the PGSs into the GP models would remove the need for stratification and allow for more adjustment precision, however, PGSs are prone to 'site' effects depending on the method and quality of genotyping and imputation... the PGSs used in this study were based on a GWAS of average bilateral HV in both male and female participants... using separate GWASs for each of these strata would potentially give the PGSs more accuracy. A second limitation of this study is the reliability of HV estimates... FreeSurfer is known to consistently overestimate HV... other brain regions with higher SNP heritability like the cerebellum or whole brain volume may show more sensitivity on nomograms. Moreover, a recent study of PGS uncertainty revealed large variance in PGS estimates, which may undermine PGS-based stratification... while NeuroCombat has been shown to remove most site effects, some may remain... there is a possibility that our results suffer from edge effects. For example, we suspect that the peak noted in the male nomogram is likely due to under-sampling in the younger participants.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study used PGS-based stratification (top and bottom 30%) to create genetically adjusted nomograms, providing a balance between training size and performance. Multiple PGS p-value thresholds (14 total: 1E-8 to 1.0) were tested, with 0.75 achieving best overall performance. Specificity of HV-PGS was validated by showing that ICV-PGS and AD-PGS did not meaningfully shift nomograms. The analysis examined both cross-sectional percentile distributions and longitudinal trajectories. Separate analyses were conducted for left, right, and bilateral mean HV, as well as sex-stratified models. NeuroCombat harmonization modeled 58 batches (UKB as one batch, 57 ADNI sites) with covariates ICV, sex, and diagnosis to preserve biological variation when combining datasets.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study is notable for being one of the first to incorporate polygenic scores reflecting healthy variation (rather than disease-associated variants like APOE) into neuroimaging normative models. The paper demonstrates that genetic factors account for substantial variance in HV even in healthy populations, and adjusting for this genetic variation can reduce phenotypic heterogeneity within diagnostic groups. The GPR approach with laGP library enabled training on consumer-grade hardware (2.3 GHz 8-Core Intel Core i9) with ~1 hour training time for 16,000 samples. The top and bottom 20% of PGS accounted for 41% of HV variance. The study compared GPR against the sliding window approach (SWA) from Nobis et al., 2019, demonstrating superior age range coverage and data efficiency. Genetic adjustment had greater impact on CN subjects than on MCI or AD subjects, likely because pathological HV loss in AD (~804 mm³ or 6.4%) far exceeds the genetic adjustment shift (~100 mm³ or 0.8%). The authors suggest that genetic adjustment may prove more useful for early detection of subtle HV loss in presymptomatic individuals. Multiple brain hemispheres and sex strata were analyzed, showing that right HV is larger than left HV in both sexes, and male HV is larger than female HV.
